script: Why did nobody look at the Mona Lisa until it disappeared? You are Vincenzo Peruggia, and in 1911 you are a handyman at the Louvre. The painting you walk past every morning is not famous yet. Tourists ignore it. On Sunday night you hide in a storage closet and wait for the museum to empty. In the morning you lift it off four iron pegs, tuck it under your coat, and walk out the front door. Nobody notices it is gone for twenty-six hours, because the staff assume a photographer has taken it upstairs. Here's the part nobody mentions. The empty wall becomes the attraction. Crowds line up to stare at the blank space, and newspapers print that face on every front page for two years. You keep it in a trunk in your apartment, a few streets from the museum, for twenty-eight months. You get caught trying to sell it to a dealer in Florence, and you serve seven months. Italy treats you as a patriot returning stolen property. The Louvre gets the most valuable accident in history. Today it hangs behind bulletproof glass with its own guard, and millions of people a year photograph a painting nobody would look at until it disappeared.

title: A Handyman Stole the Mona Lisa in 1911. Why Did That Make It Priceless?
description:
Before 1911 the Mona Lisa was just another painting in the Louvre — tourists walked straight past it. Then a handyman named Vincenzo Peruggia hid in a closet overnight, lifted it off four iron pegs and walked out the front door with it under his coat.

The empty wall drew bigger crowds than the painting ever had.

So what actually made it priceless: the art, or the theft?
